summary: Defines the syntaxes used by LDAPv3 for attribute values and the rules for writing those values as octet strings during transmission. It was replaced by RFCs 4510, 4512, 4517 and 4523.

plainLanguage.summary: LDAP sends every attribute value as a plain byte string, so something has to say what those bytes mean. This RFC defines the syntaxes that do the saying, and lists the attribute types and object classes that servers should support.

questions: how are ldap attribute values encoded
what is an ldap attribute syntax
how is a directory string encoded in ldap
subtitle: The rules that say what the bytes in an LDAP attribute value mean.

tldr.problem: LDAP carries every attribute value as a plain string of bytes. Without a rule that says what those bytes mean, a client cannot tell a date from a name from a certificate, and a server cannot compare values correctly.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2252 defines a set of syntaxes for LDAPv3 and the rules for writing the values of those syntaxes as octet strings. It also defines the attribute types and object classes that servers should support, and the matching rules used to compare values.
tldr.outcome: The document was approved as a Proposed Standard with a note that LDAPv3 update operations needed authentication that did not yet exist. It was later obsoleted by RFC 4510, RFC 4512, RFC 4517 and RFC 4523, and updated by RFC 3377.

today: RFC 2252 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4510, RFC 4512, RFC 4517 and RFC 4523, and updated by RFC 3377. It is one of the LDAPv3 documents, alongside RFC 2251 for the protocol itself and RFC 2253 for the string form of distinguished names.

sections.title: What the RFC Defines
sections.content:
LDAP requires that the contents of AttributeValue fields in protocol elements are octet strings. RFC 2252 defines a set of syntaxes for LDAPv3 and the rules by which the values of those syntaxes are represented as octet strings for transmission. The syntaxes it defines are referenced by this and other documents that define attribute types, and the RFC also defines the set of attribute types that LDAP servers should support.

The RFC frames these definitions as the framework for developing schemas for directories. Schema is the collection of attribute type definitions, object class definitions and other information a server uses to decide how to match a filter or an attribute value assertion against the attributes of an entry, and whether to permit add and modify operations. Sections 4 to 8 give the general requirements and notation for attribute types, object classes, syntaxes and matching rules, then list the attributes, the syntaxes, the object classes and the matching rules.

The IESG note at the front of the document records a caveat. Update access requires secure authentication, but this document does not mandate any satisfactory authentication mechanism, so it was approved as a Proposed Standard only to encourage implementation and interoperability testing, to encourage read-only use, and to avoid delaying other standards-track protocols that need to query LDAPv3 directories. The note warns that clients and servers that make use of update functionality are unlikely to interoperate until mandatory authentication is standardised, and discourages deploying them in the meantime.
sections.plainLanguage: LDAP carries directory entries as lists of attributes, and each attribute holds values. This RFC supplies the vocabulary that gives those values meaning, so that two servers agree what a value means and how to compare it.

sections.title: Attribute Types and Object Classes
sections.content:
Attribute types and object classes are written in the string representation of the AttributeTypeDescription and ObjectClassDescription data types from X.501. The RFC gives a BNF for each.

An attribute type description starts with the numeric object identifier of the type and may then carry a NAME, giving the names used for it, a DESC with a description, an OBSOLETE flag, a SUP naming the attribute type it is derived from, matching rules for EQUALITY, ORDERING and SUBSTR, a SYNTAX giving the syntax of its values, and the flags SINGLE-VALUE, COLLECTIVE and NO-USER-MODIFICATION. A USAGE field says where the attribute may be used, with the options userApplications, directoryOperation, distributedOperation and dSAOperation, and the default is userApplications. Servers must implement every attribute type the RFC references, should provide at least a SUP and a SYNTAX field for each, and may recognise extra types provided they publish them in the attributeTypes attribute of their subschema entries. Attribute names are case insensitive.

An object class description has a numeric identifier, a NAME, an optional DESC and OBSOLETE flag, a SUP list naming the superior object classes, a class kind that is ABSTRACT, STRUCTURAL or AUXILIARY and defaults to structural, and MUST and MAY lists of attribute types. Every entry contains an abstract class, either top or alias, at least one structural class, and zero or more auxiliary classes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each attribute type is written as a short record. It names the attribute, says what it is derived from, names the rules used to match it in a search, and gives the syntax its values follow. Object classes work the same way and say which attributes an entry must and may have.

sections.title: Syntaxes and How Values Are Encoded
sections.content:
The encoding rules for a syntax must produce octet strings, and to the greatest extent possible those octet strings should be usable in their native form for display. Where a printable representation does not make sense, as with audio, clients must not assume that an unrecognised syntax is a string representation.

Where an arbitrary string appears inside a larger production, a backslash quoting mechanism escapes the separator character, such as a quote, a dollar sign or a hash, with a backslash followed by a pair of hexadecimal digits. A backslash in the string is always sent as \5C or \5c.

Binary transfer is the exception. When the client asks for the binary encoding of an attribute, or when the syntax name is the Binary syntax, the contents of the AttributeValue field are a BER-encoded instance of the ASN.1 data type defined for use with X.500. All servers must implement this form both for generating attribute values in search responses and for parsing values in add, compare and modify requests. Clients that ask for all attributes to be returned must be prepared to receive binary values, and should not simply display binary or unrecognised values to users.

Each syntax is named by a dotted-decimal object identifier, which is not meant to be shown to users. A suggested maximum length for a value may be appended in curly braces after the identifier in an attribute type description, as in 1.3.6.4.1.1466.0{64}, which suggests that a string of 64 characters should be allowed. The bound is a suggestion rather than part of the syntax name, and a single character of the Directory String syntax may take more than one byte, because UTF-8 is a variable-length encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Most values are written so that a person can read them straight off the wire. A special binary form exists for values that come from ASN.1 definitions, and it is the only form that always survives a round trip unchanged.

sections.title: The List of Syntaxes
sections.content:
Section 6 defines the syntaxes one at a time, from the Attribute Type Description through UTC Time. Each one gives its object identifier, its name and a rule for writing a value. Some values are human readable and some are not, and the RFC marks each entry with a column that suggests whether a value in that syntax is likely to be a human readable string. Clients and servers need not implement every syntax, and the RFC strongly deprecates the definition of arbitrary new syntaxes, because today's implementations generally cannot recognise a syntax they have never seen. In most cases an attribute is defined with the syntax for directory strings.

Several syntaxes build on others. A Country String value is encoded like a Directory String but is limited to exactly two printable characters, as listed in ISO 3166. A DN value is written in the string form defined in RFC 2253, which is not reversible to the ASN.1 encoding used in X.500 for distinguished names, because the choice of string type in each component of the name is no longer known.

Directory String is the workhorse. A value in this syntax is encoded in the UTF-8 form of ISO 10646, a superset of Unicode, and servers and clients must be prepared to receive encodings of arbitrary Unicode characters, including characters not presently assigned to any character set. A PrintableString value is encoded as itself, a TeletexString value is transliterated to its UniversalString equivalent and encoded in UTF-8, and UniversalString and BMPString values use UTF-8 directly. The form of the DirectoryString is not indicated in the protocol unless the value is carried in binary, and servers must not reject values merely because they contain legal Unicode characters outside the range of printable ASCII.
sections.plainLanguage: Section 6 defines each syntax in turn, from the attribute type description to UTC time. The most used one is Directory String, which is UTF-8 text and can hold any character, including ones no character set has claimed yet.

sections.title: Matching Rules
sections.content:
Matching rules are how a server compares attribute values with assertion values when it performs a search or a compare. They are also used to identify the value to add or delete when modifying entries, and to compare a purported distinguished name with the name of an entry. Most of the attributes in the RFC have an equality matching rule defined.

Section 8 groups the rules by the kind of filter they serve. For equality filters the assertion syntax is the same as the value syntax, and the list includes objectIdentifierMatch, distinguishedNameMatch, caseIgnoreMatch, numericStringMatch, caseIgnoreListMatch, integerMatch, bitStringMatch, telephoneNumberMatch, presentationAddressMatch, uniqueMemberMatch, protocolInformationMatch, generalizedTimeMatch, caseExactIA5Match and caseIgnoreIA5Match. Several of these treat adjoining whitespace characters the same as a single space and ignore leading and trailing whitespace. Clients must not assume that servers are capable of transliterating Unicode values.

Servers that support matching rules and the extensibleMatch filter should implement all of the rules in section 8. They may add private rules, as long as they publish them in the matchingRules attribute of their subschema entries, and if they support extensibleMatch they must publish the relationship between the rules and the attributes in the matchingRuleUse attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: A matching rule says how two values count as equal. Servers use them for search filters, for compare operations and when changing an entry. Each rule belongs to a syntax, so the rule and the values it compares always agree.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Attributes of directory entries are used to provide descriptive information about the real-world objects they represent, which can be people, organizations or devices. Most countries have privacy laws regarding the publication of information about people.

The RFC also warns about a specific trap. Turning an AttributeValue from its X.501 form into an LDAP string is not always reversible back to the same BER or DER form. The example is a distinguished name with one component whose value is the text Sam. If that value came from the TeletexString choice, the LDAP form is CN=Sam, and if it came from the PrintableString choice the LDAP form is also CN=Sam, even though the two original values were different. An application that needs to reconstruct the DER form of the value, such as one verifying an X.509 certificate, should not use the string representation of attribute syntaxes when converting a value to LDAP format, but the Binary syntax instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Two points are raised. Directory entries often describe people, so publishing them can break privacy laws. And the readable string form of a value can lose information, so anything that must rebuild the original bytes has to ask for the binary form.

items.title: NAME
items.text: The names used for the attribute type. Attribute names are case insensitive.

items.title: SUP
items.text: The attribute type this one is derived from.

items.title: SYNTAX
items.text: The syntax of the values, as an object identifier and an optional maximum length.

items.title: Matching rules
items.text: EQUALITY, ORDERING and SUBSTR name the rules used to match the attribute in a filter.

items.title: SINGLE-VALUE
items.text: Present when the attribute holds at most one value. The default is multi-valued.

items.title: USAGE
items.text: Where the attribute may be used: userApplications, directoryOperation, distributedOperation or dSAOperation.
